items.description: 社 originally named the local earth god's shrine — the altar raised on a patch of claimed ground for a village's protector spirit. The word later stretched to cover any group organized around a shared institution, which is why it equally means a shrine and a company: the modern sense kept the idea of a formal body bound to a place, not the religious content.

items.description: 者 almost never stands alone as a word; it works as a suffix stitched onto a verb or field to name whoever does it, much the way English -er turns 'teach' into 'teacher'. items.mnemonic_text: A flag (方 side) rallying an arrow's (矢) clan together: family.
items.meaning_mnemonic: That same stray <radical>arrow</radical>, still quivering in the vendor's pumpkin, turns out to be signed — feathers dyed the same color every year. Uncles, cousins, and a very unbothered grandmother converge on the fence from every <radical>direction</radical> the crossroads signpost names, each recognizing the fletching as theirs, until a whole clan is arguing over one ruined pumpkin about whose family shot it.
items.reading_mnemonic: Grandma stomps up in mismatched <reading>socks</reading>, glaring at the ruined pumpkin, and mutters <reading>ぞく</reading> under her breath before anyone else speaks — the whole family already knows exactly which cousin's arrow this is, just from the socks.

example_sentences.english: There are five people in my family.

items.mnemonic_text: Rice (米) measured with a dipper (斗): materials, a fee.
items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the baker plunges the trusted <radical>dipper</radical> into a sack of <radical>rice</radical>, its grains scattering like a tiny explosion as it comes up loaded and level. He tips it into a paper bag, marks a tally on the register, and charges by the scoop — the material measured out becomes exactly the fee you pay.
items.reading_mnemonic: A customer named <reading>Leo</reading> counts each dipper-load of rice as it clinks into his bag, muttering <reading>りょう</reading>, <reading>りょう</reading> under his breath to keep track of how many scoops he owes, until his tally and the register's total match up, scoop for scoop.

items.mnemonic_text: A jewel (王) cut along its natural grain (里): reason, logic.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>king / jewel</radical> hauls his spiked, jewel-crusted crown into the <radical>village</radical> and rams the spike into the packed earth between the paddies. From there he measures every paddy edge against the spike, rejecting any row that bends even slightly, until the whole village runs on nothing but his cold, straight-line reason.
items.reading_mnemonic: A surveyor named <reading>Reeko</reading> stands where the king planted his spike, snapping her measuring cord taut across the paddies with a sharp <reading>り</reading> every time a farmer's row drifts off the straight line.

example_sentences.japanese: 母は毎日料理します。
example_sentences.english: My mother cooks every day.
example_sentences.furigana: 母[はは]は毎[まい]日[にち]料[りょう]理[り]します。

example_sentences.japanese: 地理はとても難しいです。

example_sentences.furigana: 地[ち]理[り]はとても難[むずか]しいです。

items.mnemonic_text: A heart (心) pierced by a single resolved stroke: certainly necessary.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>heart</radical> is still hooked low and flinging its three drops of blood when a cleaver comes down and pins it flat to the altar with one diagonal slash through the middle. Nobody moves it again — a heart nailed down like that isn't optional anymore, it's simply necessary.
items.reading_mnemonic: The shrine boy who nailed it down mutters a chant over the pinned heart, tapping the blade's handle twice for luck, and it comes out as a flat little <reading>ひつ</reading> — like he's clearing his throat, <reading>hit-soo</reading>, before he can walk away.
items.description: 必 is 心 (heart) with one extra diagonal stroke slashing down across the hook from upper left to lower right. Without that slash, the three loose drops sit under a bare fishhook — that plain shape is 心 on its own. With it, the stroke pins straight through the hook, and that pinned, slashed heart is 必.

items.mnemonic_text: A woman (女) under a covering (覀): the essential point, needed.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The talent show can't start without her: the <radical>woman</radical> frozen mid-dance, one leg swung wide and arms flung across her body, is the only act the whole gym is waiting on. Every other performer gets cut from the lineup before her, because without that one dancer nothing here is important enough to keep.
items.reading_mnemonic: Backstage, the stage manager keeps checking his clipboard and groaning <reading>よう</reading>, the same sound he'd make chasing a lost <reading>yo-yo</reading> under the bleachers, because the dancer still hasn't shown up and the whole show needs her.

example_sentences.japanese: 傘が要りますか。

items.mnemonic_text: Thread (糸) running straight through the loom (圣): to pass through time.
items.meaning_mnemonic: In the temple's back room, the same <radical>right hand</radical> that keeps sneaking into the cookie jar now reaches out <radical>again</radical> and again, feeding a spool of <radical>thread</radical> through a loom staked into the <radical>earth</radical> like a signpost. Row after row, the thread passes through the frame while the monk drones the same sutra over and over, never stopping.
items.reading_mnemonic: The apprentice threading the loom is named <reading>Kay</reading>, and every time the shuttle passes through she exhales a low <reading>けい</reading>, matching the monk's chant beat for beat until the thread and the sutra finish the row together.

items.mnemonic_text: Thread (糸) sold (売) onward without a break: to continue.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane's shrine cat sleeps under its usual <radical>cover</radical>, tucked snug past its ears, but a stray <radical>thread</radical> from the blanket keeps unspooling down the mossy steps. It runs past a pair of <radical>human legs</radical> marching in place, refusing to stop, straight to the <radical>samurai</radical> duck on sentry duty, who salutes and lets the thread run on under his feet rather than break the line. Nothing here ends — it all just continues.
items.reading_mnemonic: At those same shrine steps, a tourist named <reading>Zach</reading> tries to leave but his legs won't quit marching in place, round and round, and every stomp echoes <reading>ぞく</reading> off the mossy stone, on and on, refusing to stop.

items.mnemonic_text: Two people standing side by side: to compare.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Outside Koichi's konbini, two identical clerks stand shoulder to shoulder against the doorframe, backs flat, chins level, each daring the other to be an inch taller. Neither moves, neither blinks — they just stand there side by side under the fluorescent light, forever being compared.
items.reading_mnemonic: One clerk finally cracks and jabs a thumb at himself, shouting <reading>ひ</reading> — insisting <reading>He</reading>'s obviously the taller one — while the other clerk just narrows his eyes and keeps standing there under the konbini lights, refusing to concede an inch.
items.description: 比 almost never stands alone as a word. In everyday use it shows up bound into other kanji or attached as 比べる, and mostly in contexts about ratios and percentages rather than as a freestanding term by itself.

items.mnemonic_text: Feet advancing (辶) among matched (巽) options: to choose.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The mountain trail is the same winding <radical>road</radical> you've been climbing, footsteps advancing step by step toward the summit — except today it forks three ways around the vending machine. You plant one foot on a single fork and commit, ignoring the other two. Deciding which path to advance down is what it means to choose.
items.reading_mnemonic: At that same fork, a hiker named <reading>Sen</reading> freezes completely, muttering <reading>せん</reading> over and over while staring at the vending machine, unable to advance a single step until he finally commits to a path.

items.mnemonic_text: Bones (歹) left over after the cut (戔): what remains.
items.meaning_mnemonic: At the shrine gate, the <radical>halberd</radical> that toppled when a guard's scarf snagged its blade now lies clattered in the dirt, its shaft snapped clean at the joint — a fresh crack of <radical>death / bad luck</radical> running through the wood. Nobody hauls it away; it just stays where it fell, broken but present. Whatever's left after the disaster is what remains.
items.reading_mnemonic: Every morning the shrine's groundskeeper cat, a stubborn old tom named <reading>Zan</reading>, sniffs at the broken halberd and grumbles <reading>ざん</reading>, deciding again it isn't his job to move it — so there it stays.

items.mnemonic_text: Earth (土) piled ever higher (曽): to increase.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The sun climbs behind that windowed bar marking a new <radical>day</radical>, and the farmer eyes his flooded <radical>rice field</radical> creeping past the wooden signpost planted in the <radical>earth</radical> — the plots multiplying past the marker, claiming more ground than yesterday. By sundown there is simply more of everything, mud and water both. That's increase.
items.reading_mnemonic: Back at that same signpost, a farmer named Zo watches the water creep higher up the wood and grunts <reading>ぞう</reading> each time — flat and low, like saying '<reading>zo</reading>' with a shrug. By dusk he's grunted it so many times the whole field has crept higher than the post itself.

items.mnemonic_text: Water (氵) cut down (咸) to less: to decrease.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The guard's <radical>halberd</radical> clatters down as a scarf yanks it off the gate, knocking over a cup — <radical>water</radical> flicks out drop by drop, like droplets off a wet brush, spattering into a waiting <radical>mouth</radical> below that gulps each one down. By the last drop the cup stands empty. That's decrease.
items.reading_mnemonic: Watching his cup drain past his open mouth, the guard groans <reading>げん</reading> between gulps — flat, like saying '<reading>gen</reading>' each time the water level drops. One groan per gulp, and there's less in the cup with every single one.

items.mnemonic_text: Threads (糸-like) twisted into something strange: to change.
items.meaning_mnemonic: That duckling still towed by its own bootlace, <radical>trailing foot</radical> skidding along the floor, finally snags the knob of a <radical>lid</radical> resting on a pot ahead. Everything flips — duckling and lid spin together, and when they land the lid is clamped backwards over its head like a crown. Nothing about the scene matches how it started. That's change.
items.reading_mnemonic: Watching this spin from the doorway, a chicken named <reading>Hen</reading> squawks <reading>へん</reading> in pure disbelief, the same flat sound as her own name, as the duckling waddles off wearing the pot lid like a crown.
items.description: This kanji doubles as a common na-adjective meaning strange or odd, not just change — context decides which sense is meant, and native speakers reach for that second sense constantly.

items.mnemonic_text: A dog (犬) squeezing back under a door (戸): to return.
items.meaning_mnemonic: That raccoon that rammed shoulder-first through the <radical>door</radical>, scraping its tail on the sill as it barreled into the kitchen, doesn't stop there. It circles the block, and twenty minutes later barges back through that same battered door, right where it started, tail scraping the sill all over again. That's return.
items.reading_mnemonic: Next door, a neighbor named Ray sighs <reading>れい</reading> every time he hears the door bang, flat and resigned, like counting the raccoon's laps with a low '<reading>ray</reading>'. Sure enough, a beat later, it barrels back through, right on cue.
items.description: This kanji's on'yomi is genuinely rare in modern Japanese. Outside a handful of fixed compounds, it overwhelmingly appears with its kun'yomi reading instead, so lean on that reading first in real text you encounter.

items.mnemonic_text: A body (尸) stretching (由) out to reach: to deliver, arrive.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Guests keep stepping around the sprawled <radical>corpse / body</radical>, and nobody expects him to move for the doorbell. So when a package arrives, the courier just drags the whole box across the tatami until it bumps his outstretched leg — the only way anything ever reaches him tonight. It has been delivered.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the same party, a courier named <reading>Kai</reading> keeps sighing <reading>かい</reading> as he hauls yet another box across the tatami to the sprawled body's leg, resigned to the fact that delivery here always means dragging, never handing.

items.mnemonic_text: Horns flaring above a frame of stiff crossed legs: a sheep.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look at the shape and you'll find nothing new in it: two short strokes flaring out at the top like horns, and a frame beneath locked into four stiff crossed legs. Not one stroke has been added to the <radical>sheep</radical> you already know. Standing on its own, unchanged and unbothered, it is simply a sheep.
items.reading_mnemonic: The flock's leader shoulders through the door of Koichi's konbini like a regular, and Koichi barely glances up before giving it the usual greeting: "<reading>よう</reading>!" The sheep bleats it straight back at him, <reading>よう</reading>, and heads for the onigiri shelf.
